paragraphs: One point in Fetyukovitch’s speech struck everyone. He flatly denied that the fatal three thousand roubles had ever existed, and so denied that they could have been stolen.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” he began. “Any fresh and unprejudiced observer must be struck by a peculiar feature of this case: the charge of robbery, and the complete impossibility of proving that there was anything to steal. We are told that money was stolen, three thousand roubles, but whether those roubles ever existed, nobody knows. Consider how we came to hear of that sum, and who has seen the notes. The only person who saw them, and who said they had been put in the envelope, was the servant Smerdyakov. He had spoken of it to the prisoner and to his brother, Ivan Fyodorovitch, before the catastrophe. Madame Svyetlov, too, had been told of it. But not one of these three had actually seen the notes. No one but Smerdyakov had seen them.

“Here a question arises. If the notes did exist, and Smerdyakov had seen them, when did he see them for the last time? What if his master had taken the notes from under his bed and put them back in his cash-box without telling him? Note that, according to Smerdyakov’s story, the notes were kept under the mattress. The prisoner must have pulled them out, and yet the bed was absolutely unrumpled. That is carefully recorded in the protocol. How could the prisoner have found the notes without disturbing the bed? How could he have helped staining with his blood-stained hands the fine, spotless linen with which the bed had been so carefully made?

“But I will be asked: what about the envelope on the floor? Yes, that envelope deserves a word or two. I was rather surprised just now to hear the highly talented prosecutor declare of himself (of himself, mark you) that but for that envelope, but for its being left on the floor, no one in the world would have known that the envelope and the notes in it existed, and so would not have known that the prisoner had stolen them. And so that torn scrap of paper is, by the prosecutor’s own admission, the sole proof on which the charge of robbery rests: ‘otherwise no one would have known of the robbery, or perhaps even of the money.’ But does the mere fact that that scrap of paper was lying on the floor prove that there was money in it, and that the money was stolen? Yet, it will be objected, Smerdyakov had seen the money in the envelope. But when, I ask you, when had he seen it for the last time? I talked to Smerdyakov, and he told me he had seen the notes two days before the catastrophe. Then why not imagine that old Fyodor Pavlovitch, shut up alone in impatient, hysterical expectation of the object of his adoration, may have passed the time by tearing open the envelope and taking out the notes? ‘What is the use of the envelope?’ he may have asked himself. ‘She will not believe the notes are there. But when I show her the thirty rainbow-colored notes in one roll, it will make more of an impression, you may be sure. It will make her mouth water.’ And so he tears open the envelope, takes out the money, and flings the envelope on the floor, knowing himself the owner and not worried in the least about leaving evidence behind.

“Listen, gentlemen: could anything be more likely than this theory and such an action? Why is it out of the question? But if anything of the sort could have happened, the charge of robbery falls to the ground. If there was no money, there was no theft of it. If the envelope on the floor may be taken as evidence that there had been money in it, why may I not maintain the opposite: that the envelope was on the floor because its owner had taken the money out?

“But I will be asked what became of the money, if Fyodor Pavlovitch took it out of the envelope, since it was not found when the police searched the house. In the first place, part of the money was found in the cash-box. And secondly, he might have taken it out that morning, or the evening before, to use it some other way, to give it away or send it off. He may have changed his idea, his plan of action, completely, without thinking it necessary to announce the fact to Smerdyakov beforehand. And if there is the barest possibility of such an explanation, how can the prisoner be so positively accused of murdering for the sake of robbery, and of actually carrying out that robbery? This is trespassing on the domain of the novel. If it is claimed that something has been stolen, the thing must be produced, or at least its existence must be proved beyond doubt. Yet no one ever saw these notes.

“Not long ago in Petersburg a young man of eighteen, hardly more than a boy, who ran a small business as a costermonger, walked in broad daylight into a moneychanger’s shop with an ax. With extraordinary, typical audacity he killed the master of the shop and carried off fifteen hundred roubles. Five hours later he was arrested, and, except for fifteen roubles he had already managed to spend, the whole sum was found on him. Moreover, the shopman, on returning to the shop after the murder, told the police not only the exact sum stolen but even the notes and gold coins that made it up, and those very notes and coins were found on the criminal. This was followed by a full and genuine confession from the murderer. That is what I call evidence, gentlemen of the jury! In that case I know, I see, I touch the money, and I cannot deny that it exists. Is it the same in the present case? And yet it is a question of life and death.

“Yes, I will be told, but he was carousing that night, squandering money. He was shown to have had fifteen hundred roubles. Where did he get the money? But the very fact that only fifteen hundred could be found, and that the other half of the sum could not be discovered anywhere, shows that this money was not the same money, and had never been in any envelope. By strict calculation of time it was proved at the preliminary inquiry that the prisoner ran straight from those women servants to Perhotin’s without going home, and that he had been nowhere else. So he was in company the whole time, and therefore could not have divided the three thousand in half and hidden half of it in the town. It is just this consideration that has led the prosecutor to assume that the money is hidden in some crevice at Mokroe. Why not in the dungeons of the castle of Udolpho, gentlemen? Is this supposition not really too fantastic and too romantic? And observe, if that supposition breaks down, the whole charge of robbery is scattered to the winds. For in that case, what could have become of the other fifteen hundred roubles? By what miracle could they have disappeared, since it is proved that the prisoner went nowhere else? And we are ready to ruin a man’s life with such tales!

“I will be told that he could not explain where he got the fifteen hundred that he had, and that everyone knew he was without money before that night. Who knew it, I ask you? The prisoner has given a clear and unflinching account of where that money came from. If you will have it so, gentlemen of the jury, nothing could be more probable than that account, or more consistent with the temper and spirit of the prisoner. The prosecutor is charmed with his own romance. A man of weak will, who had brought himself to take the three thousand so insultingly offered by his betrothed, could not, we are told, have set aside half of it and sewn it up. Even if he had done so, he would have unpicked it every two days and taken out a hundred, and would have spent it all within a month. All this, you will remember, was put forward in a tone that allowed no contradiction. But what if the thing happened quite differently? What if you have been weaving a romance, and about quite a different kind of man? That is just it: you have invented quite a different man!

“I will be told, perhaps, that there are witnesses that he spent the whole three thousand given him by his betrothed in one day, a month before the catastrophe, so that he could not have divided the sum in half. But who are these witnesses? The value of their evidence has already been shown in court. Besides, in another man’s hand a crust always looks bigger, and not one of these witnesses counted that money. They all judged simply by sight. And the witness Maximov has testified that the prisoner had twenty thousand in his hand. You see, gentlemen of the jury, psychology is a two-edged weapon. Let me turn the other edge now and see what comes of it.

“A month before the catastrophe the prisoner was entrusted by Katerina Ivanovna with three thousand roubles to send off by post. But the question is this: is it true that they were entrusted to him in such an insulting and degrading way as was proclaimed just now? The young lady’s first statement on the subject was different, perfectly different. In the second statement we heard only cries of resentment and revenge, cries of long-concealed hatred. And the very fact that the witness gave her first evidence incorrectly gives us the right to conclude that her second evidence may have been incorrect also. The prosecutor will not, dares not (his own words) touch on that story. So be it. I will not touch on it either. I will only venture to observe that if a lofty, high-principled person, such as that highly respected young lady unquestionably is, if such a person, I say, allows herself suddenly to contradict her first statement in court, with the obvious motive of ruining the prisoner, then it is clear that this evidence has been given neither impartially nor coolly. Have we not the right to assume that a revengeful woman may have exaggerated a great deal? Yes, she may well have exaggerated, in particular, the insult and humiliation of her offering him the money. No, it was offered in such a way that it was possible to take it, especially for a man as easy-going as the prisoner, and above all because he expected to receive shortly from his father the three thousand roubles that he reckoned was owing to him. It was thoughtless of him, but it was just his irresponsible thoughtlessness that made him so confident that his father would give him the money, that he would get it, and so could always send off the money entrusted to him and repay the debt.

“But the prosecutor refuses to allow that on the same day he could have set aside half the money and sewn it up in a little bag. That is not his character, he tells us; he could not have had such feelings. Yet he himself spoke of the broad Karamazov nature. He cried out about the two extremes that a Karamazov can contemplate at once. Karamazov is just such a two-sided nature, swinging between two extremes, that even when moved by the most violent craving for riotous gaiety, he can pull himself up if something strikes him on the other side. And on the other side is love, that new love which had flamed up in his heart, and for that love he needed money, oh, far more than for carousing with his mistress. If she were to say to him, ‘I am yours, I will not have Fyodor Pavlovitch,’ then he must have money to take her away. That was more important than carousing. Could a Karamazov fail to understand it? That anxiety was just what he was suffering from. What is there improbable in his laying aside that money and hiding it in case of emergency?

“But time passed, and Fyodor Pavlovitch did not give the prisoner the expected three thousand. On the contrary, the prisoner heard that his father meant to use this sum to seduce the woman he, the prisoner, loved. ‘If Fyodor Pavlovitch does not give the money,’ he thought, ‘I shall be put in the position of a thief before Katerina Ivanovna.’ And then the idea came to him that he would go to Katerina Ivanovna, lay before her the fifteen hundred roubles he still carried round his neck, and say, ‘I am a scoundrel, but not a thief.’ So here we already have a twofold reason why he should guard that sum of money as the apple of his eye, why he should not unpick the little bag and spend it a hundred at a time. Why should you deny the prisoner a sense of honor? Yes, he has a sense of honor. Granted that it is misplaced, granted that it is often mistaken, yet it exists and amounts to a passion, and he has proved that.

“But now the affair becomes even more complicated. His jealous torments reach a climax, and those same two questions torture his fevered brain more and more: ‘If I repay Katerina Ivanovna, where can I find the means to go off with Grushenka?’ If he behaved wildly, drank, and made disturbances in the taverns in the course of that month, it was perhaps because he was wretched and strained beyond what he could endure. These two questions became so acute that they drove him at last to despair. He sent his younger brother to beg for the last time for the three thousand roubles. Without waiting for a reply, he burst in himself and ended by beating the old man in the presence of witnesses. After that he had no prospect of getting the money from anyone, for his father would not give it to him after that beating.

“The same evening he struck himself on the breast, on the upper part of the breast where the little bag was, and swore to his brother that he had the means of not being a scoundrel, but that still he would remain a scoundrel, for he foresaw that he would not use that means. He said he would not have the character, he would not have the will-power, to do it. Why, why does the prosecutor refuse to believe the evidence of Alexey Karamazov, given so genuinely and sincerely, so spontaneously and convincingly? And why, on the contrary, does he force me to believe in money hidden in a crevice, in the dungeons of the castle of Udolpho?

“The same evening, after his talk with his brother, the prisoner wrote that fatal letter, and that letter is the chief, the most stupendous proof that the prisoner committed robbery! ‘I shall beg from everyone, and if I do not get it I shall murder my father and take the envelope with the pink ribbon on it from under his mattress as soon as Ivan has gone.’ A full program of the murder, we are told, so it must have been he. ‘It has all been done as he wrote,’ cries the prosecutor.

“But in the first place, it is the letter of a drunken man, written in great irritation. Secondly, he writes about the envelope from what he had heard from Smerdyakov, again, for he had not seen the envelope himself. And thirdly, he wrote it indeed, but how can you prove that he did it? Did the prisoner take the envelope from under the pillow? Did he find the money? Did that money indeed exist? And was it to get money that the prisoner ran off, if you remember? He ran off post-haste not to steal, but to find out where she was, the woman who had crushed him. He was not running to carry out a program, to do what he had written, that is, not for an act of premeditated robbery. He ran suddenly, spontaneously, in a jealous fury. Yes! I will be told, but when he got there and murdered him, he seized the money, too. But did he murder him after all? The charge of robbery I repudiate with indignation. A man cannot be accused of robbery if it is impossible to state exactly what he has stolen. That is an axiom. But did he murder him without robbery? Did he murder him at all? Is that proved? Is that, too, not a romance?”
